lines.text: In 1731, Philadelphia had no lending library, no fire company, no hospital and no college.
By 1751 it had all four, and Benjamin Franklin had helped to found each of them.
Franklin was a printer, writer, scientist and inventor.
He later signed both the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution, one of six men to sign both.
Much of his civic work followed one method: identify a public need, then meet it by pooling contributions from many members.
The method began with the Junto, a club of Philadelphia tradesmen that Franklin organised in 1727 for reading and debate.
In 1731 he proposed that members pool their money to buy books: fifty subscribers paid forty shillings each, then ten shillings a year.
The Library Company of Philadelphia still operates today and is regarded as America's oldest cultural institution.
In 1735, Franklin's newspaper published his letter on fire safety, which argued that an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure.
The next year he organised the Union Fire Company, thirty volunteers who kept their own leather buckets and turned out for fires.
In 1751, Doctor Thomas Bond proposed a hospital for the sick poor, and Franklin designed its financing.
The Pennsylvania Assembly would grant two thousand pounds only if private donors first raised the same amount.
The donors met the target. The Pennsylvania Hospital became one of the first uses of a matching grant in America.
The same year, Franklin's academy opened. It later became the University of Pennsylvania.
Each institution had to be built from nothing: its rules written, its members recruited and its money raised.
Franklin did this four times while running a printing business, publishing an almanac and conducting his experiments with electricity.
A founder today does not have to start from nothing.
A fiscal sponsor gives a new project an existing legal and financial structure. From day one it can accept tax-deductible gifts, apply for grants and sign contracts, while the founder does the work.
Mulvium is building that structure for the next Franklin.
The next great expansion of human creativity will come from making it easier to create institutions.
